# Empirical Performance Verification & Algorithmic Analysis

**Project Title:** Smart Autocomplete and Typo Correction Engine  
**Course Code:** CS302 / DSA-3 Capstone Mini Project Evaluation  
**Auditor:** Senior Performance Engineer & Academic Evaluator  
**Measurement Methodology:** Repeated empirical sampling using `std::chrono::high_resolution_clock` across 50 trials per query workload  

---

## 2. In-Depth Algorithmic Performance Analysis

### A. Prefix Autocomplete Scaling
1. **Linear Scan Scaling ($\Theta(N)$):**  
   The measured execution time of Linear Dictionary Scanning scales directly in proportion to the number of words $N$:
   - At $N = 1,000$: $3.66 \text{ μs}$
   - At $N = 5,000$: $17.35 \text{ μs}$ ($4.74\times$ increase)
   - At $N = 10,000$: $32.88 \text{ μs}$ ($8.98\times$ increase)
   - At $N = 25,000$: $81.05 \text{ μs}$ ($22.14\times$ increase)
   - At $N = 50,000$: $163.96 \text{ μs}$ ($44.80\times$ increase)  
   This closely aligns with the theoretical time complexity $O(N \cdot P)$.

2. **Trie Prefix Search Scaling ($O(P + S)$):**  
   In contrast, Trie search time remains sub-microsecond for small to medium dictionaries ($0.25 \text{ μs} - 0.62 \text{ μs}$). As $N$ expands to 50,000 words, search time only rises moderately to $3.13 \text{ μs}$. This moderate increase is attributed solely to the size of the matching subtree $S$ (more words share prefixes like `"pro"`, requiring more nodes to be visited during the DFS candidate collection step) and cache line capacity, **not** because unrelated dictionary branches are inspected.

3. **Speedup Multipliers:**  
   The measured speedup ranges from **12.17x** on small 1,000-word lexicons to a peak of **68.45x** on 5,000-word lexicons, stabilizing around **52.5x** at 50,000 words.

---

### B. Typo Correction & Branch Pruning Efficiency
1. **Linear Brute-Force Levenshtein ($O(N \cdot M \cdot \bar{L})$):**  
   At 50,000 words, computing edit distances against every dictionary word takes **4,635.18 μs (~4.6 ms)**. For a real-time keystroke event, a 4.6 ms delay noticeably consumes CPU cycles and limits concurrency.

2. **Trie DP Traversal with Branch Pruning ($O(\text{Unpruned Nodes} \cdot M)$):**  
   At 50,000 words, Trie DP typo correction executes in **170.26 μs (0.17 ms)**, delivering a **27.22x speedup**.  
   *Why is Trie DP faster?*
   - **Prefix Amortization:** Words sharing common prefixes share the exact same top rows of the DP matrix. In linear scanning, these rows are re-computed for each word; in Trie DP, they are computed once at the ancestor nodes.
   - **Branch Pruning:** As soon as $\min(\text{currentRow}) > 2$, the algorithm immediately prunes that Trie branch. On a 50,000-word tree, this eliminates $>98\%$ of all paths within the first 2 or 3 character levels.

## 3. Memory Profiling & Cache Locality Analysis

| Metric | 1,000 Words | 5,000 Words | 10,000 Words | 25,000 Words | 50,000 Words |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Trie Node Count** | 3,275 | 16,207 | 32,887 | 80,969 | 159,128 |
| **Nodes per Word Ratio** | 3.28 | 3.24 | 3.29 | 3.24 | 3.18 |
| **Estimated Trie RAM** | 0.81 MB | 3.99 MB | 8.10 MB | 19.95 MB | 39.25 MB |
| **Raw Text File Size** | 10.2 KB | 52.4 KB | 106.8 KB | 272.1 KB | 558.4 KB |

### Space-Time Trade-off:
- Each `TrieNode` consumes approximately 248 bytes ($26 \times 8$ bytes for `std::unique_ptr` array, 1 byte for `isEndOfWord`, 4 bytes for `frequency`, and 32 bytes for `std::string` storage).
- The ratio of nodes per word remains remarkably constant at $\approx 3.2$, demonstrating strong prefix sharing (common English word prefixes like `pre-`, `con-`, `pro-`, `de-`, `re-`).
- While the Trie requires ~39.2 MB of heap memory for 50,000 words compared to ~0.6 MB for a flat text array, modern desktop systems possess ample RAM, making this trade-off worthwhile for the substantial search and typo speedups.
